questions.title: How could the district court dismiss all claims with prejudice if the summary-judgment motions only addressed statutory compliance?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture. The opinion says the parties filed summary-judgment motions "related solely to whether GoAuto’s procedure for cancelling the financed insurance policies satisfied Louisiana law," but then says that once the district court found compliance with the statute, it dismissed all claims against GoAuto with prejudice. Why does winning that one statutory issue automatically dispose of the misrepresentation and bad-faith claims too? Is the idea that all of the plaintiffs' other theories depended on the cancellation being ineffective, or is there some separate procedural reason the court could enter final judgment on all claims?

questions.title: Why was Jenkins able to appeal the cancellation issue when he was not the insured whose policy was financed and cancelled?
questions.question_body: The facts say Jenkins was injured in an accident involving a third GoAuto insured who is not a party here, and that insured had financed the policy through APAC. Williams and Wright were former insureds themselves, but Jenkins seems different: he is a third-party accident victim. I'm having trouble understanding his legal posture. Is his claim basically that the other driver's policy should have still been in force because the cancellation was ineffective, so he would have coverage to recover against? If so, does Louisiana law generally let a third-party claimant challenge whether an insurance cancellation complied with the premium-finance statute?

questions.title: Does 'certifying' in Louisiana's premium-finance cancellation statute require a signature by a natural person?
questions.question_body: The main merits issue seems to be whether APAC's cancellation request had to be signed before GoAuto could cancel the policy. The Fifth Circuit says the statute requires a "statement certifying" certain facts, but does not expressly require a signature, and the court did not want to add requirements under the banner of "strict adherence." I'm struggling with that reasoning. In ordinary legal usage, doesn't a certification usually imply that some identifiable person or entity is formally attesting to the truth of the statements? How can a document be treated as a statutory certification if it is automatically generated, unsigned at the time of cancellation, and does not identify any individual employee? Is the court basically treating the company itself as the certifying actor because the statute refers to the premium finance company rather than an employee?

questions.title: How can the court demand 'strict adherence' to the statute while still allowing substantial flexibility in what counts as a certification?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly quotes Louisiana cases saying there must be strict adherence to the premium-finance cancellation procedures and that any defect makes the cancellation ineffective. But then the Fifth Circuit seems fairly pragmatic when it says a signature is unnecessary because the statute does not explicitly mention one. I'm confused about the level of formalism here. If Louisiana requires strict compliance, why isn't the absence of a signature or named certifier treated as a fatal defect? Is the court drawing a line between strictly following requirements that are actually written in the statute and refusing to infer extra formalities from the word "certifying"? If so, how is that different from a more lenient substantial-compliance approach?

questions.title: What counts as 'receipt' by the insurer when the cancellation request is sent by email and processed automatically by software?
questions.question_body: The statute says that "[u]pon receipt" of the notice of cancellation and certified statement, the insurer shall consider cancellation requested and may proceed to cancel. The Fifth Circuit holds that GoAuto had receipt once the email hit GoAuto's computer system and the system automatically cancelled the policy, even though no human reviewed the request until later that morning. I'm unsure how to think about "receipt" here. Is the court effectively saying that delivery to an insurer's server or web service is the same thing as receipt by the insurer itself? Does that mean actual human awareness is irrelevant so long as the insurer's system has possession, custody, or control of the message? I'm wondering whether this is a broad principle of electronic receipt or something tied specifically to this statute.

questions.title: Why didn't the court certify the statutory-interpretation questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs asked the Fifth Circuit to certify the meaning of terms like "certifying" and "receipt" to the Louisiana Supreme Court, arguing that the questions matter to Louisiana's insurance system and apparently have not been directly answered by the state high court. Given that federal courts are supposed to be careful under Erie when state law is unsettled, I'm confused why the Fifth Circuit was so quick to decide the issues itself. What is the standard for certification in this context? Is the absence of directly controlling Louisiana Supreme Court precedent normally not enough by itself, and did the panel think the text and lower Louisiana cases gave a sufficiently reliable answer?

questions.title: Why did the Fifth Circuit reject the district court's 'private carrier' theory instead of affirming on that alternative ground too?
questions.question_body: The district court apparently reasoned that the APAC employee physically delivering the printed notices could qualify as a "private carrier," which would satisfy the statutory method of sending the cancellation materials. The Fifth Circuit called that interpretation "imaginative and unconventional" and chose not to rely on it because the email already satisfied the statute. I'm trying to understand the appellate reasoning here. If an appellate court can affirm on any ground supported by the record, why not also decide whether the private-carrier theory works? Was the panel avoiding an unnecessarily broad interpretation of Louisiana law, especially since it was sitting in diversity and there was no Louisiana authority on point?
